source.author: verg
source.text: Inde ferarum vastatorem Amycum, quo non felicior alter ungere tela manu ferrumque armare veneno, et Clytium Aeoliden et amicum Crethea Musis, Crethea Musarum comitem, cui carmina semper et citharae cordi numerosque intendere nervis.
source.text_original: Inde ferarum / vastatorem Amycum, quo non felicior alter / ungere tela manu ferrumque armare veneno, / et Clytium Aeoliden et amicum Crethea Musis, / Crethea Musarum comitem, cui carmina semper / et citharae cordi numerosque intendere nervis.
source.text_english: Then came Amycus, ravager of wild beasts, second to none in anointing weapons by hand and arming iron with poison; and Clytius, son of Aeolus, and Crethea, friend of the Muses, Crethea, companion of the Muses, who always had songs and the cithara at heart, and to draw measures from the strings.

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: Protinus Inachiis ultro Tirynthius Argis advolat, Arcadio cuius flammata veneno tela puer facilesque umeris gaudentibus arcus gestat Hylas: velit ille quidem, sed dextera nondum par oneri clavaeque capax.
reuse.text_original: Protinus Inachiis ultro Tirynthius Argis / advolat, Arcadio cuius flammata veneno / tela puer facilesque umeris gaudentibus arcus / gestat Hylas: velit ille quidem, sed dextera nondum / par oneri clavaeque capax.
reuse.text_english: Straightway the Tirynthian flies of his own accord to Argos of Inachus, where Hylas carries for him the poisoned darts and the bows that delight his eager shoulders—Arcadian weapons: he would indeed wish it, but his right hand is not yet equal to the burden, nor able to bear the club.
